To decorate (someone or something) by surrounding with accessories, etc.
Of dangers, difficulties, enemies, etc.: to negatively affect (someone or something); to trouble.
d.x: Track and platforms have been upgraded, but refurbished trains from Vivarail have been beset by software problems.

beset.e: From Middle English besetten, bisetten (“to besiege, blockade; to fill, occupy; to harass, beset; to allot, bestow; to arrange, manage; to place, set; to provide for; to treat in a certain way”), from Old English besettan, bisettan (“to surround, beset; to set near; etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisattjan, from Pro …

d.g: An imperative uttered as a mildly imprecatory or merely expletive introductory exclamation.
d.x: Beshrew your heart, fair daughter!

beshrew.e: From Middle English beschrewen (“to curse, pervert”). By surface analysis, be- + shrew.

d.g: To beset or surround with armed forces for the purpose of compelling to surrender, to lay siege to, beleaguer.
To beleaguer, to vex, to lay siege to, to beset.
To assail or ply, as with requests or demands.

besiege.e: From Middle English besegen, bisegen, equivalent to be- (“around, about”) + siege.

d.g: To smear over, to smear all over, to daub.
To damage the reputation of, to tarnish, to sully.
d.x: His public record is already besmeared with tawdry divorces, […]

besmear.e: From Middle English *bismerwen, from Old English besmirwan, besmierwan (“to besmear”), equivalent to be- + smear. Cognate with Dutch besmeren (“to besmear”), German beschmieren (“to besmear”).

d.g: To make dirty.
To tarnish something, especially someone's reputation.
d.x: The newspaper was on a campaign to besmirch the actor.

besmirch.e: From Middle English besmorchen (attested in besmorchid). Compare Middle English bismotered (“bespattered, soiled”). By surface analysis, be- + smirch.

d.g: To muddle, stupefy, or cause to act foolishly, as with alcoholic liquor or infatuation.
d.x: You expect me and my men to besot ourselves with your drugs, ...

besot.e: From be- + sot. Compare to Middle English assoten, assotten (“to act foolishly; fall madly in love, become infatuated”).

d.g: To cover something with spangles.
d.x: He it was who had bespangled the soils with russet leaves and reeds and who had breathed the breath of life into beings.

bespangle.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English spangle English bespangle From be- + spangle.

d.g: To spatter or cover with something; sprinkle with anything liquid, or with any wet or adhesive substance.
To soil by spattering.
d.x: The flour bespattering Squeaker's now neglected clothes spoke eloquently of his clumsy efforts at damper making.

d.g: To asperse with calumny or reproach; shend.

bespatter.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English spatter English bespatter From be- + spatter.

d.g: To speak for beforehand; engage in advance; make arrangements for; order or reserve in advance.
d.x: concluding, naturally, that to gratify his avarice was to bespeak his favour

d.g: To stipulate, solicit, ask for, or request, as in a favour.
d.x: to bespeak a calm hearing

d.g: To betoken; show; indicate; depict; foretell; suggest; allude to.
d.x: This act bespeaks his kindness.

d.g: To speak up or out; exclaim; speak.

bespeak.e: From Middle English bespeken, bispeken, from Old English *bespecan, besprecan (“to speak about, speak against, accuse of, claim at law, complain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisprekan (“to discuss, blame”), from Proto-Germanic *bisprekaną (“to speak about, discuss, blame”), equivalent to be- + speak. …

d.g: To add speckles.
d.x: Seen from the air at night, tiny villages bespeckle the Indian landscape with firefly glows.

bespeckle.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English speckle English bespeckle From be- + speckle.

d.g: To make spots on; mark with spots; cover with or as with blots or blemishes.

bespot.e: From Middle English bespotten, equivalent to be- + spot.

d.g: scatter with liquid;  wet lightly

besprinkle.e: From Middle English bisprenklen, bisprenglen, bispringlen, equivalent to be- + sprinkle.

d.g: Alternative form of bestialize.
To make like a beast.
To bring or reduce to the state or condition of a beast.
To put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigor.
To make active; to rouse oneself.
d.x: The old man and his wife bestirred themselves to make every thing ready for the unexpected guests, […]

d.g: To apply or make use of (someone or something); to employ, to use.
d.x: All the voide time, that is betwene the huores of woorke ſlepe and meat, that they be ſuffered to beſtowe, euerye man as he lyketh beſte hym ſelfe.

d.g: To impart (something) gratuitously; to present (something) to someone or something, especially as a gift or an honour; to confer, to give, to accord; to render.
d.x: I bestow upon you the name of Peter.

bestow.e: PIE word *h₁epi The verb is derived from Middle English bestowen, bistouen, bistowen (“to give, bestow; to apply (something to something else); to arrange or have control over (something); to place (someone) in a position; to use (for some purpose); (reflexive) to find (oneself) a place to live or shelter”) [and other …

d.g: To strew or scatter about; throw or drop here and there.
To strew anything upon; strew over or about; cover or partially cover with things strewn; cover with straw or strewing.

bestrew.e: From Middle English bistrewen, from Old English bestrēawian, bestrēowian (“to bestrew, besprinkle”), equivalent to be- + strew. Cognate with Dutch bestrooien (“to sprinkle, bestrew”), German bestreuen (“to sprinkle, cover”), Swedish beströ (“to strew, sprinkle, scatter”).

d.g: To be astride something, to stand over or sit on with legs on either side, especially to sit on a horse.
d.x:
& thou were the truest frende to thy louar that euer bestrade hors
"And thou were the truest friend to thy lover that ever bestrad horse"

d.g: To stride over, or across.
To dominate.
d.x: Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus[…].

bestride.e: From Middle English bestriden, from Old English bestrīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *bistrīdan; equivalent to be- + stride. Compare Dutch bestrijden, German bestreiten.

d.g: To think of (something or somebody) or that (followed by clause); to remind oneself, to consider, to reflect upon.
d.x: Baſ[ſanio]. Be aſſured you may. / Iew [i.e., Shylock]. I will be aſſured I may: and that I may be aſſured, I will bethinke mee, may I ſpeake with Anthonio?

d.g: To meditate, ponder; to consider.
To determine, resolve.

bethink.e: From Middle English bethenken, bithenchen (“to think about, consider”) from Old English beþenċan, biþenċan (“to think upon, remind, consider, remember”), from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną; equivalent to be- + think. …

d.g: Often used in a prediction (chiefly in woe betide) or a wish: to happen to (someone or something); to befall.
d.x:
Why, how now, countrymen!
Why flock you thus to me in multitudes?
What accident's betided to the Jews?

d.g: Chiefly in the third person: to happen; to take place; to bechance, to befall.
d.x: If he were dead what would betide of me.

betide.e: From Middle English bityden [and other forms]; from bi- (prefix forming verbs, usually with a completive, figurative, or intensive sense) + tyden (“to come about, happen, occur; to befall, become of, happen to (someone); to be the fate of (someone); to await (someone); to fare, get along”); tyden is derived from Old En …

d.g: To signify by some visible object; show by signs or tokens.
d.x: There be other 2 signes in often use of which the first is made thus + and betokeneth more : the other is thus made – and betokeneth lesse.

d.g: To foreshow by present signs; indicate something future by that which is seen or known.
d.x: “ Ah ! hospitable land, thou (nevertheless) betokenest war,” i. e., although hospitable, thou nevertheless betokenest war. — Bello.

betoken.e: From Middle English bitoknen, bitacnen, from Old English betācnian (“to betoken, signify, designate”), from Proto-West Germanic *bitaiknijan. Equivalent to be- + token. …

d.g: To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust; to give up treacherously or faithlessly.
d.x: An officer betrayed the city.

d.g: To prove faithless or treacherous to, as to a trust or one who trusts; to be false to; to deceive.
d.x: to betray a person or a cause

d.g: To violate the confidence of, by disclosing a secret, or that which one is bound in honor not to make known.
To disclose (a secret, etc.) in deliberate violation of someone’s confidence.
d.x:
The dead leap at the throat, destroy
The meaning of the day; dark forms
Have scaled your walls, and spies betray
Old secrets to amorphous swarms.

betray.e: From Middle English betrayen, bitrayen (“to commit an act of treason against”), equivalent to be- + tray (“to betray”). Middle English bi- is from Old English be- (“be-”), from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”), from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near, by”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi (“at, near”). …

d.g: give to in marriage

betroth.e: From Middle English bitrouthen, bitreuthen (“of a man: to pledge to marry; to give (a woman) in marriage, arrange the marriage of”), from bi- (prefix forming transitive verbs from nouns) + trouth, treuthe (“faithfulness, fidelity, specifically marital fidelity; promise, undertaking, specifically a promise of marriage; …

d.g: To wail over; to feel or express deep sorrow for.
d.x:
[…] Though in this city he
Hath widow’d and unchilded many a one,
Which to this hour bewail the injury,
Yet he shall have a noble memory.

bewail.e: From Middle English bewailen, equivalent to be- (“over, about”) + wail.

d.g: To use caution, pay attention to (used both with and without of).
d.x: Behold, I send an Angel before thee[…]. Beware of him, and obey his voice.

beware.e: From Middle English bewar, be war, be ware, forms of Middle English ben ware (“to be on one's guard, be vigilant”, literally “be ware”), equivalent to be + ware or be + aware. Compare Old English bewarian.

d.g: To give or add whiskers to; to put whiskers on.
d.x: Cinema magnates preferred to bewhisker the handsome profile and contort the slender Barrymore frame to suit weird, melodramatic parts then in vogue.

d.g: To confuse, disorientate, or puzzle someone, especially with many different choices.
d.x: All the different possible options may bewilder us.

bewilder.e: From be- (prefix used as an intensifier) + wilder (“to lead astray; to go astray, wander”).

d.g: To cast a spell upon.
d.x: Afterwards Jim said the witches bewitched him and put him in a trance,[…]

d.g: To fascinate or charm.
d.x: I was bewitched by the sight of the girl dancing in the forest.

d.g: To astonish, amaze.
d.x: Is it not a fact that the miners of this country are bewildered and bewitched and do not know what is to happen?

bewitch.e: From Middle English bewicchen, bewycchen, biwicchen, equivalent to be- + witch.

d.g: To reveal, divulge, or make (something) known; disclose.
d.x: His countenance bewraies he is displeasd.

d.g: To reveal or disclose and show the presence or true character of, especially if unintentionally or incidentally, or else if perfidiously, prejudicially, or to one's discredit.
d.x:
He tooke hir fast betwéene his armes, and not without his shame,
Bewrayed plainly what he was and wherefore that he came.

d.g: To expose or rat out (someone).
d.x: And after a while came unto him they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee.

bewray.e: From Middle English bewraien, bewreyen, biwreyen, from Old English *bewrēġan, from Proto-Germanic *biwrōgijaną (“to speak about; tell on; inform of”). …
